_comment: The mutation gate's declaration: which files are mutation-graded, and which suites pin them. It is the only source for that pairing — the per-run Stryker config and the vitest include are both generated from it (`mutation-check.ts`), so there is no second list to keep in step. Entries arrive one at a time and deliberately: adding one asserts that the named suites, on their own, pin that file's behaviour, and the gate will say so in numbers on the next change to it. Asserted in full by `__tests__/mutation-scope.test.ts`, because a shrinking list is how this gate would pass by grading less.

equivalents.why: The guard exists to narrow `state` from `string | undefined` before it indexes the status map; it decides nothing the next line does not already decide. Without it an absent or empty state produces no mapped status, and `if (!externalStatus) return null` two lines down returns null for exactly the same inputs. No payload can tell the two apart, because there is none where the first guard returns and the second would not.

equivalents.line: if (highest === undefined || highest < count) known.executions.set(line, count)
equivalents.why: The comparison keeps the highest count a shard reported. With `<=` an equal count overwrites an equal count, which stores the same number it replaced. No input can distinguish the two, so no test can.

equivalents.line: if (best === undefined || best < count) executions.set(line, count)
equivalents.why: The same maximum, taken over the statements starting on one line. `<=` replaces an equal value with an equal value.

The component name is metadata on a log line and reaches no branch, no return value and no query. A test could only assert the string back from the logger it just configured, which is the tautology the mutation gate exists to expose rather than to reward.
Same line, same reason: the component name is log metadata, not behaviour. The line's operator-facing content that does matter — the post id in the warning — is asserted in post-source.db.test.ts.

The selected row is never read: hasActiveGitLabLink returns whether one came back, not what was in it. Narrowing or widening the projection cannot change that boolean, so no input distinguishes the two.

The guard only spares a throw the catch beside it absorbs: new URL rejects null, undefined and the empty string alike, and both paths end at the same gitlab.com default. Measured on all three falsy values.

Two constraints upstream already hold what the predicate checks: the query selects only mappings whose targetKey is this board, and completeRuleOf returns no rule unless filters.boardIds[0] equals that same targetKey. Every rule that reaches find therefore has boardId === boardId, so no stored row makes the predicate decide anything.
Only the number of queries changes. With no links, buildIssueMoveTargets returns the same empty list the short circuit returns, so the guard saves a lookup and decides nothing.

The shortcut and the general form build predicates that mean the same thing. Falling through yields `NOT assigned OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 ... AND <empty inArray>)`, and drizzle renders an empty `inArray` as the literal `false` (measured on 0.45.2), so the EXISTS is unsatisfiable and the OR collapses back to `NOT assigned` for every row. No entry, product or reader can be arranged where the two disagree, because they are the same predicate written twice. The branch is kept rather than deleted because the general form only reduces correctly through that empty-inArray rendering, which is drizzle's choice and not ours to rely on.

`defaultMessage` is the English written beside a message id, and react-intl reads it only when the active catalogue has no entry for that id. Every id in a shipped source file is in all nine catalogues -- that is what `bun scripts/i18n-check.ts` fails the build over -- so the catalogue always wins and this string never reaches a screen. A test could only assert it by rendering against a catalogue that lacks the id, which is the state the i18n gate exists to make impossible. It stays in the source as the fallback V6 promises if that gate ever stops holding, and because `bun run intl:extract` reads it.

The `$` follows a greedy `.*` that has already run to the end of the comment, and with `/s` there is no line boundary for it to stop at, so there is nothing left for the anchor to reject. Even a trailing newline the two could in principle disagree about is gone before anything reads the group: the only use of `matched[1]` trims it.

`start` is the offset of a comment, so `text[start]` is `/` and `text[start + 1]` is `*` or `/`. The backwards search for a newline therefore finds the same newline whether it begins one character before the comment or one character inside it, because a comment opens with two characters and neither of them can be a line break.

equivalents.line: const after = text.slice(end, lineEnd < 0 ? text.length : lineEnd)
equivalents.why: The branch is taken only when no newline follows the note, and what this line computes is read only through `ownLine`, which decides whether the note also speaks for the line below it. A line below exists only if a newline follows. So the mutant changes the answer exactly in the case where nothing can ask the question.

equivalents.line: const after = text.slice(end, lineEnd < 0 ? text.length : lineEnd)
equivalents.why: `lineEnd` is `indexOf('\n', end)` for a comment that ends past position 0, so it is either -1 or greater than 0. Zero is the one value the two comparisons disagree about, and it is the one value this search cannot return.

The fallback stands for a callee with no name of its own -- `window.self.alert`, where the object is itself a member expression -- and it is asked of a set holding one name. Any string that is not that name answers identically, so no source can tell the empty string from another absent name.

The same shape one line down, for a method reached by a computed key such as `toast['error']`, where the property has no name. The set holds three names and any other string answers the same, so the empty string is not distinguishable from another absent name.

Forced true, every node still reaching this line enters the branch, and the line inside it sends back an empty list for anything whose operator is not `+`. The one other node that carries `+` as an operator is a unary plus, which has no `left` and no `right`, so it spreads two empty lists -- the same empty list the fall-through below returns. The condition was split out of an `&&` for this record's sake: joined, three mutants shared the line and the manifest addresses a line by its text.

The operator-facing content of the hook's log lines — the project, the status and GitLab's answer — is asserted in hook.test.ts; the child's name is the one field a test could only read back from the logger it just configured.
Same line, same reason: the component name is log metadata, not behaviour, and the payload of every line the hook writes is asserted separately.

The second argument of history.replaceState is the entry's title, which the HTML specification tells browsers to ignore and no browser reads. The URL is the third argument and is asserted; nothing observable — not the location, not the history length, not the document title — changes with the second.

The guard above makes the header a non-empty string, and String.prototype.split returns at least one element for any input, so index 0 is always a string (an empty one for a leading comma) and the optional call never short-circuits. The `?.` satisfies the indexed-access type; no request reaches the undefined it guards against.

Same line, same reason: the component name is log metadata, not behaviour.

Node reads a falsy input encoding as its default, utf8, so the digest of the same string is byte-for-byte the same: createHash('sha256').update('abc', '') and update('abc', 'utf8') both give ba7816bf...15ad (checked on Node 22 and on bun). No code can observe which spelling of the default was used.

Same line, same reason: the component name is log metadata, not behaviour.

Splitting on a single separator instead of a run of them differs only in the empty strings it emits between adjacent separators and around a leading or trailing one, and the filter on the same line removes every empty string. For any input the two produce the same token list.

The fallback is only read when the scope parameter is absent. isFullAsCatalogue is true for exactly one token set, the eleven authorization-server scopes, and neither the empty string nor a three-word sentence is that set, so both fall through to parsing the absent parameter as no scopes at all.

The child logger's component name is log metadata: every code path behaves the same with or without it, and no test reads the logger's bound fields. Same reason as the widget-install-pairing and install-context records.

storage() returns null only when window is missing or localStorage access throws. Without the optional chaining that null becomes a TypeError inside the same try block, whose catch returns [] — the value the original returns for a null storage as well. Both paths yield 'nothing remembered'.
Emptying the catch leaves raw at its initial null, and the very next line returns [] for a null raw. A throwing getItem therefore still reads as 'nothing remembered'.

Skipping the null/empty guard sends null or '' into JSON.parse: null parses to null, which fails the Array.isArray check on the next line and returns [] as well; '' throws SyntaxError, which the surrounding catch turns into []. Every input reaches the same result.

Without the array guard a parsed object, string, number or boolean reaches .filter, which does not exist on any of them; the TypeError is caught by the surrounding catch and read as []. Only an array passes either way.
When storage() is null the mutant throws a TypeError inside the try block whose catch deliberately swallows storage failures, so the recording is dropped exactly as the original drops it.
The false arm of a.emoji ? … : -1 is unreachable: matches is filtered on item.emoji two lines above, so every item compared here has a glyph. The comparator never evaluates the constant.
Same unreachable false arm for b: both operands of the comparator come from the glyph-filtered list.

Never taking the guard evaluates window.localStorage where window is not declared, which throws a ReferenceError inside the try block on the next line, and that catch returns the same null the guard returned. In a browser the guard is false anyway. Both environments therefore reach the identical null, and every caller reads null as "storage unavailable".

typeof never yields the empty string, so comparing against it makes the guard permanently false. That is the same code path as the ConditionalExpression record on this line, and it ends at the same null by the same route through the catch.

Entering the block when neither item is remembered runs straight into if (aRecent === -1) return 1, so the comparator answers 1 where it answered 0. Both answers say "do not put a ahead of b", and the sort is stable, so no arrangement can show the difference. Measured rather than assumed, because the mutant also makes the comparator inconsistent: 540,000 arrangements (60,000 each at lengths 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 16, 40, 80 and 200) sorted identically under V8.

The second operand can only decide the entry when the first one is false, that is when aRecent === -1 — and that is exactly the case the block answers with its first statement, return 1. Dropping the operand therefore answers 0 where the original answered 1, which a stable sort reads the same way. Measured rather than assumed, because the mutant also makes the comparator inconsistent: 540,000 arrangements (60,000 each at lengths 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 16, 40, 80 and 200) sorted identically under V8. Two further mutants share this address, replacing the whole condition and its first operand with false; both are caught by "orders exact, then remembered by recency, then prefix, then the rest (G5)", and that test, not this record, is what holds them. A record is only consulted for a mutant that survived, and one matching no survivor fails the run as stale.

Flipping the second comparison changes the entry only where the first operand is false, so again only where aRecent === -1, and there the block answers 1 while skipping it answers 0. Measured rather than assumed, because the mutant also makes the comparator inconsistent: 540,000 arrangements (60,000 each at lengths 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 16, 40, 80 and 200) sorted identically under V8.

The -1 in the second comparison is reachable only when the first one is false, so changing it swings the entry only where aRecent === -1, and there the block answers 1 against the 0 of skipping it. Measured rather than assumed, because the mutant also makes the comparator inconsistent: 540,000 arrangements (60,000 each at lengths 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 16, 40, 80 and 200) sorted identically under V8. Its sibling on this line, aRecent !== +1, shares the address and is a different matter: with aRecent a real index and bRecent === -1 the block reaches if (bRecent === -1) return -1, and -1 against 0 does move an element. It is caught by "a remembered exact match wins even when it is not the most recently used glyph (G5)", and by the property test beside it.

The mutant drops the third operand, so a stored 'portal' falls through to the line below — which returns 'portal'. The clause is deliberately redundant with the fallback: it keeps all three audiences named where a reader looks for them, rather than leaving 'portal' to be inferred from the default. No value can tell the two apart, because the two answers are the same string.

Skipping the guard only matters for a token whose last '.' is at index 0 or absent, and neither reaches a non-null answer. With no dot the signature compared is the whole token against the HMAC of its own first n-1 characters, which is a fixed point of HMAC-SHA256 and not constructible. With the dot at index 0 the payload is the empty string, whose signature is computable, but that payload then carries no separator and `if (sep <= 0) return null` two lines down refuses it. Both paths end in null, as the guard intended.

The two differ only when the last '.' sits at index 0. That token can be built — the payload is the empty string and this key signs it — but an empty payload carries no separator, so `if (sep <= 0) return null` refuses it on the next branch. The answer is null either way.

A signed payload with no separator, or one starting with it, is the only thing this guard answers. Past it, `withoutExpiry` is either the payload minus its last character or the empty string, and neither holds a separator either — so `if (scopeSep <= 0) return null` refuses it. Reaching that far at all needs a payload that parses as a future timestamp, and it still ends in null.
The two differ only for a payload whose last separator is at index 0, which leaves `withoutExpiry` empty; `scopeSep` is then -1 and the audience guard below refuses it. Null either way.

`Buffer.from(string, 'base64url')` does not throw: characters outside the alphabet are ignored rather than rejected, and `toString('utf8')` does not throw either. So no token reaches the catch, which is why it reports as never executed rather than as a survivor. The guard is upstream's and it is kept, because those two calls are the attacker-controlled part of this function.
